target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Third Army: gasoline shortage threatens a halt before the Meuse
chunk_text: General Patton took his supply problem to General Bradley's headquarters the following day but was told that the Third Army could expect no appreciable amount of gasoline until 3 September. General Gay wrote: "If this is correct ... the Third Army is halted short, of its objective, the Meuse River."
source_title: U.S. Army: The Lorraine Campaign, Chapter I
rationale: The passage focuses on gasoline shortage threatens a halt before the Meuse.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Third Army: air delivery temporarily averts an operational halt
chunk_text: Gasoline was the one item which was essential to further movement by the Third Army. The first severe impact of the supply shortage on Patton's operations had been staved off for a brief period when, on 26 and 27 August, over a thousand planes were used to fly gasoline and rations to the Third Army.
source_title: U.S. Army: The Lorraine Campaign, Chapter I
rationale: The passage focuses on air delivery temporarily averts an operational halt.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Third Army: gasoline allocation leaves formations immobilized
chunk_text: The priority on gasoline which bad been assigned the First Army, in consequence of General Eisenhower's decision to make the main Allied effort in the north, left the Third Army virtually immobilized from 1 to 5 September. During the period 26 August-2 September the gasoline received by the Third Army averaged 202,382 gallons per day.
source_title: U.S. Army: The Lorraine Campaign, Chapter I
rationale: The passage focuses on gasoline allocation leaves formations immobilized.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: U.S. armor: tanks drop out and pursuit cannot resume
chunk_text: Individual tanks were dropping out of combat formations for lack of gasoline. The chance of a speedy resumption of the pursuit east of the Meuse, a hope that depended on motorized columns, appeared nil.
source_title: U.S. Army: Breakout and Pursuit, Chapter XXXI
rationale: The passage focuses on tanks drop out and pursuit cannot resume.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: German armor: fuel shortage prevents a division moving for 36 hours
chunk_text: On 21 December the 2d SS Panzer Division was ordered to relieve the 560th Volks Grenadier Division in the battle at Fraiture but was unable to move for thirty-six hours because there was no POL. In the Fifth Panzer Army there were reports as early as 19 December of a "badly strained" fuel situation.
source_title: U.S. Army: The Ardennes: Battle of the Bulge, Chapter XXV
rationale: The passage focuses on fuel shortage prevents a division moving for 36 hours.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Germany: pilot training and panzer movement curtailed
chunk_text: For lack of fuel, pilot training, previously cut down, was further curtailed. Through the summer, the movement of German Panzer Divisions in the field was hampered more and more seriously as a result of losses in combat and mounting transportation difficulties, together with the fall in fuel production.
rationale: The passage focuses on pilot training and panzer movement curtailed.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Ardennes offensive: inadequate reserves and reliance on captured fuel
chunk_text: By December, according to Speer, the fuel shortage had reached catastrophic proportions. When the Germans launched their counter-offensive on December 16, 1944, their reserves of fuel were insufficient to support the operation. They counted on capturing Allied stocks.
rationale: The passage focuses on inadequate reserves and reliance on captured fuel.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Japan: fuel scarcity prevents large fleet operations
chunk_text: A. The fleet fuel situation became very acute early in this year. Our surface units were restricted even as to their training activities, and any large-scale operation requiring heavy supplies of fuel became almost out of the question.
source_title: USSBS: Interrogation NAV 75, Admiral Toyoda Soemu
rationale: The passage focuses on fuel scarcity prevents large fleet operations.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Japan: fuel and personnel shortages limit air opposition
chunk_text: The Japanese have lost many of their best air leaders—most of their experienced pilots and large numbers of their maintenance crews. They are also very short of gasoline and oil. As a result, Army and Navy planes operating over Hokkaido, Honshu, and the Ryukyus rarely encounter more than 70 or 80 planes.
source_title: FRUS Potsdam Conference, Volume II, document 710a-90: military briefing on Japan, 24 July 1945
rationale: The passage focuses on fuel and personnel shortages limit air opposition.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Japan: fuel shortages impede fleet operations and pilot training
chunk_text: Q. About what time during the course of the war was the operation of the fleet or the use of planes for training or operations first seriously inconvenienced by shortage of fuel? A. About two or three months before the MARIANAS Campaign we felt the shortage very keenly.
source_title: USSBS: Interrogation NAV 55, Vice Admiral Ozawa Jisaburo
rationale: The passage focuses on fuel shortages impede fleet operations and pilot training.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Italy: fuel shortage prevents fleet activity
chunk_text: Though a close watch was kept on all the Italian bases, their fleet never showed signs of serious activity. It was seriously handicapped by shortage of fuel.
source_title: The War at Sea, 1939–1945, Volume II, Chapter XIX
rationale: The passage focuses on fuel shortage prevents fleet activity.

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Malta: Ohio’s fuel cargo enables air strikes to restart
chunk_text: Their efforts were finally crowned with success, when the grievously wounded, almost unmanageable but still indomitable Ohio entered harbour. The fuel which she carried enabled air strikes to be restarted from Malta just when Rommel was preparing for the offensive intended to drive the Allies finally out of Egypt.
source_title: The War at Sea, 1939–1945, Volume II, Chapter XIII
rationale: The passage focuses on Ohio’s fuel cargo enables air strikes to restart.

chunk_text: Five days after the supposed settlement of the oil-rail center controversy, Spaatz proposed that thirteen synthetic oil plants in Germany be attacked as third priority, coming after the German Air Force and the rail centers. chunk_text: On the following day, 21 April 1944, Doolittle had 864 heavy bombers and 1,040 fighters scheduled to begin the oil offensive. But rapidly deteriorating weather conditions at the bases and target areas compelled him to cancel the mission.
source_title: The Army Air Forces in World War II, Volume III, Chapter 6

target_anchor: Oil and fuel constraints on operations
coverage: Exclusion: attacks on synthetic oil plants
chunk_text: The Eighth Air Force returned to the oil offensive on 28 May 1944, when more than 400 heavies bombed synthetic oil plants at Ruhland, Magdeburg, Zeitz, Merseburg-Leuna, and Lützkendorf, all of them damaged targets still suffering from the raids of 12 May. Results were good everywhere.
